AMR-X Mobile Base Platform

Led the mobile-base sub-team on a modular AMR platform — configuring the ROS 2/Nav2 stack and shaping the chassis design.

ROS 2 · Nav2SLAMTeam Lead

Role

Intern on the Autonomous Navigation team; team lead of the Mobile Base Platform sub-group (Group 02 — Mobility & Internal Arrangement) at CyberMech Systems / CMS Vortex Labs LLC, Tunis — a 2-month internship, working alongside teammate Meriem, under supervisor Hamza Abderrahmen. AMR-X is a modular differential-drive mobile robot: a common base that accepts interchangeable modules (manipulator arm, shelf-access module, compartment, sensor module) to cover several use cases without multiplying platforms.

Perception: filtering & fusing two LiDARs

AMR-X carries two RPLIDAR A2M12 units mounted on diagonally opposite corners for full 360° coverage — but each one also sees a slice of the robot's own chassis. Self-detections had to be filtered out, otherwise the robot draws itself as an obstacle and the planner thinks it's boxed in. A distance-threshold filter was tried first but blinded the robot to real walls in narrow corridors, so the fix instead masks the exact angular sectors where each LiDAR sees the chassis (one LiDAR needed two sectors, since its blind spot straddled the ±180° wrap-around). The two cleaned scans are fused into a single 360° scan in the robot's base frame, feeding SLAM, the costmaps, and the collision monitor. Filtering was verified by checking the minimum range of the fused scan rather than assumed: a value near the chassis radius meant a leftover blind spot.

Mapping (SLAM) and localization (AMCL)

  • Mapped a simulated warehouse and a hospital environment with SLAM Toolbox, always confirming a single publisher was writing to /map before saving, and visually inspecting each map for clean, continuous walls before trusting it.
  • Diagnosed a subtle bug where the live LiDAR scan drifted off the map's walls as soon as the robot moved, even though localization looked correct at a standstill. Traced it to two compounding causes: the wheel separation had been computed from the URDF joint origins, but the SolidWorks-to-URDF export had offset the wheel meshes 1.89 cm inside those origins, so the real wheel base was larger than assumed and the robot physically turned faster than odometry reported; and AMCL was only correcting its estimate every 0.25 m / ~11° of motion. Recalculating the wheel separation from the mesh geometry, tightening AMCL's update thresholds, and feeding it the fused scan together eliminated the drift (rotation later verified accurate to within 1%).
  • Contributed to the CAD → URDF pipeline feeding the simulation model, including manually adding joint frames after SolidWorks' automatic export proved unreliable.

Costmaps, planning & safety

  • Paired a NavFn global planner with an MPPI local controller, plus a velocity smoother and collision monitor; fixed a stuck-robot issue in narrow corridors caused by an oversized inflation radius merging the costmap halos of both walls.
  • Built keepout-zone masks (aligned to each saved map) around stairwells and other drops a 2D LiDAR can't see, so the planner refuses those areas outright instead of driving the robot in.
  • Developed a mission-server node exposing topics/services to send the robot to named stations or raw coordinates (including multi-stop routes), report progress, cancel a goal, and save the current pose as a new named station — each goal is checked against the costmap before being sent, so an unreachable target is rejected immediately rather than exhausting Nav2's recovery behaviors.
  • Validated the full stack against 19 static obstacles and 16 dynamic pedestrian actors added to the simulated hospital but absent from the SLAM map, confirming the local costmap detects and routes around them in real time.

Mechanical contribution

Ahead of the navigation work, contributed to the suspension design for AMR-X's drive wheels and payload plate (comparing wire-rope isolators and polyurethane mounts to protect ride quality and onboard sensors), and helped debug the CAD-to-simulation pipeline that later explained the odometry drift above.

Mobile base platform design

  • Benchmarked competitor AMR platforms ahead of the design phase.
  • Generated an AI-assisted concept design via Zoo Design Studio.
  • Finalized a 4-caster-wheel configuration for the base.
  • Resolved a pending LiDAR placement question together with the ROS team.

Market research

  • Authored a comprehensive AMR market research report (PDF and LaTeX) covering global market sizing, competitor landscape, and Tunisia/MENA feasibility.
  • Flagged Enova Robotics (Sousse) as the key direct competitor.
  • Identified Tunisia's automotive manufacturing supply chain (LEONI, Aptiv, Valeo, Yazaki) as the strongest near-term pilot target.

INSAT End-of-Year Project (PFA) · 2025–2026

Quadruped Corrosion-Inspection Robot

A Wi-Fi-controlled quadruped built to inspect corrosion — spanning mechanical design, embedded control, and computer vision.

SolidWorksESP32Computer Vision

Overview

Final-year engineering project (PFA) at INSAT, Industrial Computing & Automation, with teammates Aziz Hizem, Amira Merzougui, and Manar Afli, supervised by Mme. Imen Jaafar. A Wi-Fi-controlled quadruped built to inspect corrosion on industrial metallic surfaces — walking on a mechanically-validated 3D-printed chassis while a separate AI pipeline scans the live video feed for rust. Manual visual inspection is slow and sometimes hazardous to run on real equipment; the goal was a low-cost legged platform that combines locomotion and detection in one system instead of treating them separately.

Mechanical design

Fully 3D-printed PLA quadruped chassis modeled in SolidWorks 2023 — a 28×25×5 cm body plate and four identical three-segment legs, 12 DOF total from twelve MG995 servos (Coxa/Femur/Tibia per leg). FEA in SolidWorks Simulation under conservative loads (4 kg body mass, 1.4 N·m servo torque — double the rated value) returned safety factors from 6.3 up to roughly 100 across the three most-loaded printed parts, comfortably clearing the 1.5 threshold used to sign off the design.

Locomotion — designed vs. shipped

The plan was a closed-form inverse-kinematics solver (foot position → hip/knee/foot joint angles, solved analytically in ~10 µs with reachability and singularity checks) driving a 12-phase Creep Gait that shifts the center of gravity before lifting each leg, keeping three feet grounded at all times without needing an IMU. Partway through integration the Pololu Mini Maestro 12 servo controller developed a UART fault, and swapping in a PCA9685 PWM driver over I2C to fix it ate into the time left to get that IK/gait pipeline actually running on the ESP32. Rather than ship nothing, the team hand-recorded three gait sequences in the Maestro GUI (forward: 15 frames, backward: 17, turn: 15, at 350 ms/frame) and baked them into firmware as fixed PWM arrays played back by a simple sequencer. The robot walks and turns reliably on a flat floor with three-leg ground contact held at every step — but it's fixed-sequence locomotion, not the adaptive gait originally designed; the IK math is fully derived and ready to drop in whenever that work resumes.

Wi-Fi control

The ESP32 runs as its own Wi-Fi access point, serving a lightweight HTML control page (Forward / Backward / Turn / Stop) straight from flash — no dedicated app, sub-100 ms response over the local link.

Computer vision

A YOLOv11n model trained on a public Roboflow corrosion dataset (8,178 images across 13 categories) for real-time rust detection — 0.419 mAP@50 overall, with the two sharpest-contrast categories individually above 0.84, at 2 ms inference per frame. Fully validated offline against recorded video and a webcam; the ESP32-CAM module wasn't available during the integration window, so the vision pipeline never actually ran on the walking robot's own camera feed — closing that loop would just mean pointing the existing inference script at the camera's stream URL.

Simulation & validation

A PyBullet environment with A* path planning, occupancy-grid mapping, and an autonomous navigator, used earlier in the project to validate behavior before committing to hardware.

Documentation

A full LaTeX report, including a cover page rebuilt to match INSAT's institutional template.

NXP Cup Tunisia · 2026

NXP Cup Tunisia — Autonomous Race Car

Programmed an autonomous race car on an NXP microcontroller for Tunisia's national student competition.

NXP MCUEmbedded CCompetition

Overview

Programmed an autonomous race car on an NXP microcontroller for NXP Cup Tunisia 2026, the local round of NXP's international student competition where entrants build and code a self-driving vehicle to complete a track entirely on its own — no remote control, no human intervention once the run starts.

Competition format

Season 2025/2026 rules: teams of one to three students of any grade level, one car per team, built around any NXP-brand MCU or MPU — NXP's official 2025 3D-printed kit, a legacy kit (Alamak, Model-C, DFRobot, MR-BUGGY3), or a fully custom build, all racing head-to-head in the same category regardless of hardware. The car has to navigate primarily by camera — an optical sensor for line-following is mandatory — and has to be genuinely autonomous during the race itself: any wireless link has to be physically unplugged before the car goes anywhere near the track, with connectivity allowed only for diagnostics during development.

The track & the race

Cars run on a 7×4 m serpentine circuit, a 55 cm-wide lane bounded by a continuous black edge line, with intersections crossing at 45° or 90° — and the layout is only revealed shortly before the event, so there's no training on the actual course. After the car clears the first two curves on its opening lap, a 20×20×20 cm white foam "end of race" obstacle appears somewhere on the straight ahead; the car has to recognize it, slow down hard, and stop within 10 cm of it without touching it. Each team gets three timed attempts and keeps the time from its first clean lap rather than its fastest, so a single spin-out on attempt one costs nothing but a re-run. Scoring stacks a lap-time ranking (up to 650 points for the fastest car of the event) with a separate 150-point bonus for sticking the stop.

IEEE RAS INSAT · 2025

ECPP 2.0

Embedded-systems competitive-programming contest organized by IEEE RAS INSAT.

Embedded SystemsC/C++STM32IEEE RAS

Overview

ECPP 2.0, organized by IEEE RAS INSAT, is a mini hackathon built around a simple loop: solve, code, win. Teams are handed a set of problems to tackle directly on an STM32 board, with the goal of producing firmware that's both functional and optimized within a tight time limit.

Format

Teams of 4 to 6 people work on the STM32 Discovery F407 board and have a single 4-hour window to deliver working code. The hackathon itself runs offline: no WiFi is available once the clock starts. To compensate, teams are free to download anything they might need beforehand — GitHub repos, datasheets, reference code — and use it locally during the event.

MATLAB · 2024

AI-Based Beamforming

An LSTM network trained to steer an antenna's beam toward its optimal direction.

MATLABLSTMSignal Processing

Overview

Personal and Professional Project (PPP) at INSAT, done with two teammates (Meher Lahouar, Mohamed Amine Medini) under Mr. Naoufel Ismail: predicting a beamforming antenna's received signal power as a function of scanning angle, given a desired signal angle and two interferer angles, using deep learning instead of the usual analytical formulas.

Approach

Compared two architectures on the same 4-input, 1-output regression task (desired angle, two interference angles, scanning angle → power in dB): a feedforward network (3 hidden layers of 10 neurons, trained with Levenberg–Marquardt) and an LSTM (50 hidden units, Adam optimizer, 100 epochs). The interesting part is that the LSTM's usual strength — learning sequences — was repurposed here: the four inputs aren't a time series, but sweeping the scanning angle from 0° to 20° still forms an ordered, parametric sequence the LSTM can exploit. Each model was implemented and trained twice, once in MATLAB (Deep Learning Toolbox) and once in Python (TensorFlow/Keras), to compare the two ecosystems on the same task.

Results

The LSTM outperformed the FFNN in both implementations, correctly reproducing the reference power curve's main lobe and the sharp interference nulls. The Python implementation edged out MATLAB on every metric while training roughly 3× faster:

  • MATLAB LSTM: MAE 3.48, RMSE 4.25, R² 0.977, trained in ~266 s.
  • Python LSTM: MAE 2.64, RMSE 3.40, R² 0.985, trained in ~92 s.
